what_it_does: Training giant AI language models requires shuffling enormous datasets stored in a compressed, column-organized file format called Parquet. Reading those files one random item at a time is over 100 times slower than reading them in bulk, because the format is designed for bulk access, not for the random-access pattern that shuffling demands. YOUMU is a data-loading pipeline that sidesteps this mismatch by reading data at the smallest natural unit inside a Parquet file — a single compressed page of a few kilobytes — so every disk read is useful and no data needs to be converted to a different format first.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Parquet files are organized in large chunks (hundreds of megabytes each). When training software asks for random training examples, the system must read an entire chunk to get just a few rows — wasting 99.9% of the bandwidth. Modern solid-state drives (SSDs) are actually efficient at smaller random reads, down to their natural page size (a few kilobytes). YOUMU exploits that: it accesses data at page granularity rather than chunk granularity.

How it works. At startup, YOUMU scans the Parquet metadata — no data is read yet — and builds a Global Page Index: a directory that maps every page across all files to its exact physical location on disk and its decompression instructions. Shuffling is done by randomly permuting a list of page IDs; a layered binary search translates each random ID into the file, chunk, and page needed, using only the in-memory index. The data plane then reads exactly that one page from the SSD, decompresses it on the fly using the metadata, and converts it to an array. An aggressive buffer strategy continuously refills a fixed-size in-memory queue as pages are consumed, shuffling rows inside the buffer with each new arrival — giving two levels of randomness (page order and within-buffer row order) while keeping memory use constant regardless of dataset size.

The key design choice. Operating at page granularity unifies the disk-access unit with the shuffle unit, eliminating the mismatch. No format conversion is ever needed; the original Parquet files are used directly.

The result. On a 200-billion-token dataset across 16 machines, YOUMU uses up to 82% less RAM than the best alternative (Ray Data), achieves the same throughput, and delivers model training accuracy almost indistinguishable from a perfect random shuffle — whereas the widely-used streaming approach degrades accuracy severely on some datasets.
